newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK-Trade data, auction announcement.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK-Trade data, auction announcement.

text.p: June U.S. trade figures, dollar and stock market performance, the terms of the next Treasury note auctions and technical factors could influence U.S. government securities trade on Wednesday, analysts said.

The Commerce Department releases June U.S. trade data at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT. Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that the U.S. had a $10.36 billion trade deficit in June, slightly wider than the $10.23 billion trade deficit recorded for May.
The impact of the trade data on the bond market, however, is difficult to determine, analysts said.

"Typically (the trade report) is not a market mover and the reason for that is that it can be interpreted for its implications either for the dollar or for GDP (Gross Domestic Product)," said John Williams, managing director and chief global markets economist at Bankers Trust.

"It's a mixed bag," he said. "A bigger trade deficit means a weaker GDP - which is good for bonds. But it also might mean a weaker dollar - which is bad for bonds. So there is always a schizophrenic reaction to a change in the trade deficit."
Josh Stiles, senior bond analyst at I.D.E.A., agreed.

"If the trade deficit is up a little bit or down a little bit, it might not have much impact," said Stiles. "Anyway, the market never knows how to interpret that report. What might hurt the dollar could (shrink) GDP."

The bond market will continue to watch the performance of the U.S. dollar in foreign exchange markets and the action of the U.S. equity market, analysts said. The yield curve should at least hold steady following the stock market's recovery from its 247-point slide on Friday, analysts said. The Dow rose 108.7 points on Monday and 114.74 points on Tuesday.
The spread between 2- and 30-year yields ended at 67 basis points on Tuesday, down from Friday when flight-to-quality buying steepened the curve to 73 basis points.
The Treasury Department's afternoon announcement of the terms of its next two- and five-year note auctions will also be a matter of interest to dealers, analysts said.
Participants expect the Treasury to say that it will sell $15.5 billion in two-year notes next Tuesday and $11.5 billion in five-year notes on August 27.
Technical factors will also influence trade, they said.

Traders located psychological resistance at 6.50 percent on the 30-year bond yield. The 6.50 percent yield closely corresponds to 114-16 on the September bond contract, a level that would represent a 50 percent retracement of the down move to 111-31 from 116-31, said Stiles.
"That slide was pretty swift because it began the day after month-end when all the books got squared away and the economic data didn't really support where we were," he said.
In addition, 114-15 represents the 20-day moving average on the September T-bond, said Stiles.
"That makes it a tough little hurdle," he concluded.
Big support for the bond yield lies at 6.66 percent, he said.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond ended at 98-07, up 4/32 to yield 6.51 percent.
Dealers indicated that Federal funds would open near 5-7/16 percent.
